bull_bear.body:
- Scale and market leadership: #1 organised eye care provider in India by revenue and the most geographically diversified chain, with the highest number of surgical eye care facilities (199) and the highest number of facilities in tier-1 cities (87) in India, per CRISIL Intelligence.
- Asset-light hub-and-spoke operating model: the Company owns only one facility and leases all other locations, reducing capital intensity and allowing flexible expansion into various geographical areas while sharing doctor and medical resources across the network.
- Clinical talent moat in a supply-constrained market: 968 doctors and 2,189 paramedical staff, with exclusive full-time contracts with the majority of doctors, against an industry in which India has on average around 1.5 ophthalmologists per 100,000 population.
- Clinical innovation record: an uninterrupted record of surgical innovations developed within the network (Phakonit, Glued IOL, PDEK, CAIRS, Single-Pass Four-Throw Pupilloplasty, Pinhole Pupilloplasty, Temporary Pupil Scaffolding) presented at ASCRS, AAO and APAO and adopted widely in different parts of the world.
- Clinical governance: a dedicated Clinical Board chaired by Dr. Soundari that sets clinical benchmarks, supported by four specialist committees (Quality Control, R&D, Education, Drug and Medical Devices) and two advisory boards, including a Speciality Advisory Board of 28 experts across nine specialised services.
- Repeatable expansion playbook: 152 facilities added organically and 52 through strategic acquisitions since FY22, with a disciplined and repeatable playbook for launching and scaling greenfield facilities enabling faster ramp-up and improved operating leverage.
- High industry entry barriers - capital-intensive infrastructure, limited specialist talent, entrenched brand loyalty and complex regulatory compliance.
- In-house AI-ready hospital management system 'Neo', designed and developed internally and built to scale for over 5,000 branches and 2 million patients per day, integrating clinical, operational and patient workflows with real-time visibility into patient volumes, waiting times and inventory.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Medical and clinical risk inherent to a surgery-led model — The MD&A states that risks are classified as medical and non-medical, with dedicated senior management personnel appointed as risk officers. Surgical procedures remain the largest contributor to revenues (3,23,245 surgeries in FY26, of which 73.0% were cataract), so adverse clinical outcomes or quality lapses strike the primary revenue engine directly; the Quality Control Committee runs regular clinical audits to monitor outcomes and identify adverse events.
- Litigation risk explicitly monitored by the Board — The MD&A records that while no existential threats are identified, the Board monitors material risks such as litigation, fire incidents and regulatory changes. For a healthcare provider this is structural rather than episodic, given the clinical nature of the services delivered across 288 facilities.
- Regulatory and compliance risk — Named by the Board as a monitored material risk alongside litigation and fire incidents, and identified in the MD&A as an industry-level entry barrier arising from complex regulatory compliance. Regulatory categories are formally listed among the risk categories the Board-overseen framework addresses.
- Scarcity of ophthalmology talent constraining growth and inflating cost — The MD&A flags the paucity of healthcare personnel in the Indian eye care industry as a key entry barrier: India had approximately 20,944 ophthalmologists and 17,849 optometrists as of 2025, about 1.5 ophthalmologists per 100,000 population, with only around 2,750 PG ophthalmology seats offered annually. Because the Company depends on exclusive full-time contracts with the majority of its 968 doctors, this constrains the pace at which new facilities can be staffed and is a stated HR risk category.
- Geographic concentration in South India — The South region contributed 61.2% of FY26 domestic revenue mix and holds 182 of the 269 Indian facilities, against 16.4% for West, 9.2% for North and 2.9% for East. Management explicitly frames diversification away from a predominant South India presence as a strategic objective, making regional concentration a structural exposure while that rebalancing is underway.
- Execution risk on a rapid, largely greenfield expansion programme — The Company added 57 facilities organically in FY26 and closed five primary facilities, entered Delhi NCR as a new and highly competitive market, and plans 60 further facility additions in FY27. Operational and strategic risk are named risk categories in the MD&A framework; ramp-up of new facilities and integration of acquisitions carry execution exposure that the vintage-performance disclosure shows is real (FY26-vintage facilities contributed only 2.4% of revenue).
- Asset-light leasing model concentrates exposure in lease obligations and site availability — The Company owns only one facility and leases all other locations. While this reduces capital intensity, it makes the network dependent on securing and retaining suitable leased infrastructure - infrastructure and location availability is one of the five criteria used to identify growth clusters - and the Board framework names financial risk as a monitored category.
- International operations across nine African countries — 19 facilities across Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique, Mauritius, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Ghana and Madagascar are held through the Orbit Healthcare Services (Mauritius) chain and contributed 10.1% of revenue from operations, with a new Ethiopian subsidiary to commence shortly. The Directors' Report discloses foreign exchange earnings and outflow and a foreign subsidiary reporting in MUR, so cross-border and currency exposure sits alongside the operating risk of multiple jurisdictions.
- Dependence on a single integrated technology platform — The Company operates on a common, integrated technology platform - the in-house AI-ready hospital management system Neo - providing doctors and paramedical staff access to patient data across the network including clinical diagnosis, surgical history and payment records. Information and cyber security risks are expressly within the Risk Management Committee's mandated risk-identification framework, and concentration on one platform holding clinical and payment data is a structural single point of failure.

- Expand the network with disciplined capital allocation while strengthening presence in key strategic markets.
- Nurture the next generation of ophthalmologists through structured recruitment, continuous skill development and growth-oriented career pathways.
- Leverage technology to improve access, affordability and patient outcomes, including the in-house AI-ready hospital management system 'Neo'.

outlook.body: Expansion for Dr. Agarwal's is footprint-led rather than plant-led: the Company runs an asset-light hub-and-spoke model in which it owns only one facility and leases all other locations, which reduces capital intensity and allows flexible expansion into new geographies. The network reached 288 eye care facilities as at 31 March 2026 - 269 in India across 14 states and 5 union territories (87 of them in tier-1 cities) and 19 in Africa across nine countries - comprising 35 tertiary facilities of 10,000-12,000 sq ft (including four Centres of Excellence at Chennai, Tirunelveli, Vashi and Jalandhar), 164 secondary surgical facilities of 5,000-7,000 sq ft and 89 primary facilities of 750-1,000 sq ft. During FY26 the Company added 57 facilities organically and none inorganically; the Directors' Report records 30 new surgical centres (5 in Karnataka, 4 each in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu, 3 in Delhi, 2 each in Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Kerala and Telangana, and 1 each in Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) and 27 new primary centres (6 each in Tamil Nadu and Odisha, 5 in Karnataka, 4 in Andhra Pradesh, 3 in Telangana, 1 each in Kerala and Maharashtra and 1 at an international location). Five primary facilities were closed in FY26. Since FY22 the Company has added 152 facilities organically and 52 through strategic acquisitions, taking the domestic network from 91 facilities in FY22 to 269 in FY26 (56 additions in the South and 11 across other regions on the FY22-FY26 comparison). New micro-markets or 'clusters' are selected by evaluating competitor dynamics, potential of scaling up, doctor and talent availability, market size and growth potential, and infrastructure and location availability. Entry into Delhi NCR during the year produced 7 facilities in under a year, with the Company stating it is investing aggressively to build a leadership position there over the next two to three years. Internationally, the Company entered Africa in 2012 and now operates 19 facilities across Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique, Mauritius, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Ghana and Madagascar, intends to add a few facilities in Africa each year, and has a new subsidiary in Ethiopia set to commence operations shortly. The stated expansion plan for FY27 is 60 facility additions. Alongside footprint growth the Company continued to upgrade its medical equipment base across facilities with deployment of robotic cataract systems, advanced microscopes and vitrectomy platforms (IOL Master 700 optical biometer, Legion phaco machine, Ziemer Femto LDV Z8 and J&J Catalys robotic femto cataract systems, and the Visumax 800 SMILE Pro refractive machine), and continued to build out its in-house AI-ready hospital management system Neo, designed to scale to over 5,000 branches and 2 million patients per day.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's healthcare delivery industry is projected to grow from Rs 7.0 Lakh Crores in FY25 to Rs 11.2-12.2 Lakh Crores by FY30P at a CAGR of 10-12%, driven by demand for routine medical treatments, elective surgeries and OPD services (per CRISIL Intelligence).
- India's eye care industry is projected to reach Rs 74,000-84,000 Crores by FY30P, growing at a CAGR of 12-14% from FY25 - one of the fastest-growing healthcare segments, though eye care is currently only about 7% of the Indian healthcare delivery market.
- The single-speciality segment is expanding faster than the overall industry, growing at a 10-15% CAGR through FY26E versus 9.8% CAGR for healthcare delivery overall, because single-speciality centres are capex-light, scalable and replicable.
- Organised eye care service chains are gaining share from standalone hospitals and clinics - from 9-11% of the market in FY20 to 14-16% in FY26E and a projected 16-19% by FY30P - on higher brand equity, standardised operations, widespread network presence and a comprehensive treatment set.
- Disease burden and demographics: India has the world's highest number of people with vision loss (about one in five affected), 40-50% of the population has refractive error, around 70% of the population above 60 suffers from cataract, and about 66% of blindness above age 50 is due to untreated cataract.
- Policy and coverage tailwinds from government schemes such as NPCB&VI and Ayushman Bharat, plus expanding health insurance penetration.
- Volume growth drivers: increased patient footfall and strengthening surgical conversions.
- Value growth drivers: a shifting mix towards high-value procedures and value-added services including newer sub-specialities, opticals and pharmacy.
- Same-store sales growth of 14.1% for all facilities set up or acquired up to FY23 evidences maturing-vintage revenue growth alongside new-facility additions.
- The Indian optical eyewear market is projected to grow at a 9-11% CAGR between FY25 and FY30P, reaching Rs 50,000-60,000 Crore by FY30P, supporting sustained demand for spectacles and contact lenses.
- Structural supply constraint on the industry cost line: India had approximately 20,944 ophthalmologists and 17,849 optometrists as of 2025, with roughly 2,750 PG ophthalmology seats offered annually - a constrained talent pipeline that also raises entry barriers.
- India's lower cataract surgery rates compared with global averages indicate significant headroom for volume growth.

Surgical procedures remain the largest contributor to revenues (3,23,245 surgeries in FY26, of which 73.0% were cataract), so adverse clinical outcomes or quality lapses strike the primary revenue engine directly; the Quality Control Committee runs regular clinical audits to monitor outcomes and identify adverse events.

risks.note: The MD&A records that while no existential threats are identified, the Board monitors material risks such as litigation, fire incidents and regulatory changes. For a healthcare provider this is structural rather than episodic, given the clinical nature of the services delivered across 288 facilities.
risks.risk: Litigation risk explicitly monitored by the Board

risks.note: Named by the Board as a monitored material risk alongside litigation and fire incidents, and identified in the MD&A as an industry-level entry barrier arising from complex regulatory compliance. Regulatory categories are formally listed among the risk categories the Board-overseen framework addresses.

The MD&A flags the paucity of healthcare personnel in the Indian eye care industry as a key entry barrier: India had approximately 20,944 ophthalmologists and 17,849 optometrists as of 2025, about 1.5 ophthalmologists per 100,000 population, with only around 2,750 PG ophthalmology seats offered annually. Because the Company depends on exclusive full-time contracts with the majority of its 968 doctors, this constrains the pace at which new facilities can be staffed and is a stated HR risk category.
risks.risk: Scarcity of ophthalmology talent constraining growth and inflating cost

risks.note: The South region contributed 61.2% of FY26 domestic revenue mix and holds 182 of the 269 Indian facilities, against 16.4% for West, 9.2% for North and 2.9% for East. Management explicitly frames diversification away from a predominant South India presence as a strategic objective, making regional concentration a structural exposure while that rebalancing is underway.

The Company added 57 facilities organically in FY26 and closed five primary facilities, entered Delhi NCR as a new and highly competitive market, and plans 60 further facility additions in FY27. Operational and strategic risk are named risk categories in the MD&A framework; ramp-up of new facilities and integration of acquisitions carry execution exposure that the vintage-performance disclosure shows is real (FY26-vintage facilities contributed only 2.4% of revenue).

risks.risk: Medical and clinical risk inherent to a surgery-led model
risks.note: The MD&A states that risks are classified as medical and non-medical, with dedicated senior management personnel appointed as risk officers. risks.risk: Litigation risk explicitly monitored by the Board
risks.note: The MD&A records that while no existential threats are identified, the Board monitors material risks such as litigation, fire incidents and regulatory changes. For a healthcare provider this is structural rather than episodic, given the clinical nature of the services delivered across 288 facilities.

Named by the Board as a monitored material risk alongside litigation and fire incidents, and identified in the MD&A as an industry-level entry barrier arising from complex regulatory compliance. Regulatory categories are formally listed among the risk categories the Board-overseen framework addresses.

risks.risk: Scarcity of ophthalmology talent constraining growth and inflating cost
risks.note: The MD&A flags the paucity of healthcare personnel in the Indian eye care industry as a key entry barrier: India had approximately 20,944 ophthalmologists and 17,849 optometrists as of 2025, about 1.5 ophthalmologists per 100,000 population, with only around 2,750 PG ophthalmology seats offered annually. The South region contributed 61.2% of FY26 domestic revenue mix and holds 182 of the 269 Indian facilities, against 16.4% for West, 9.2% for North and 2.9% for East. - [Group structure] Dr. Agarwal's Health Care Ltd holds 72.7% of listed Dr. Agarwal's Eye Hospital Ltd (27.3% public), 100% of Orbit Healthcare Services (Mauritius) Ltd which runs the Africa business and has 9 step-down subsidiaries, 100% of Aditya Jyot Eye Hospital Private Limited (balance 12.25% stake acquired in October 2025), 93.2% of Elisar Life Sciences Private Limited and 51.0% of Dr Thind Eye Care Private Limited (as on Mar 31, 2026, updated for the preferential allotment).
- [Closures] Two primary facilities were closed in Q1'FY27 - Janipur (Jammu) and Zirakpur (Punjab); in FY26, five primary facilities were closed.
- [Industry] Crisil-sourced market framing: India healthcare delivery market c. Rs 7.7 Lakh Cr growing 10-12% FY26-FY30P; India single specialty healthcare c. Rs 2.7-3.5 Lakh Cr; India eye care services market c. Rs 48,500 Cr growing 12-14% FY26E-FY30P, with eye care the fastest-growing single specialty (14% FY20-FY25 versus 6-8% to 10-12% for dental, mother-and-child, oncology and orthopaedic).
- [Payor mix] Q1'FY27 payor mix was Cash 63.6%, Insurance/TPA 27.7% and Government 8.7% (versus 61.7% / 29.1% / 9.2% in Q1'FY26); payor-mix revenue excludes subsidiary Elisar Life Sciences.
- [Elisar] Multiple disclosures (vintage performance, mature/emerging split, payor mix, regional mix) explicitly exclude revenues of subsidiary Elisar Life Sciences Private Limited, which is engaged in developing, designing, manufacturing, importing and exporting ophthalmic diagnostic devices such as auto perimeters, optical biometers and ophthalmoscopes - so those cuts do not reconcile to consolidated revenue.

one-line thesis: Dr. Agarwal's crossed INR 2,000cr revenue with 21.6% growth driven by disciplined greenfield additions (19 in Q4) and 14% same-store growth, while margin expansion to 28.9% EBITDA proves operating leverage despite INR 30cr drag from new centers. The impending merger with the listed subsidiary and aggressive FY27 capex (60 new centers) position the company to double down on North/West expansion while sustaining premiumization trends in high-end cataract and refractive procedures.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 564cr (Q4, +22.6% YoY), INR 2,080cr (FY26, +21.6% YoY); EBITDA: INR 174cr (Q4, 30.2% margin), INR 614cr (FY26, 28.9% margin, +31bps); PAT: INR 50cr (Q4, +17.4%), INR 168cr (FY26, +52.4%); Order Book: N/A (Service sector); Net Debt: Reduced by INR 195cr via IPO proceeds; One-offs: INR 80lakhs merger expenses in Q4, INR 3.3cr incremental Facebook marketing spend, INR 1cr corporate office rent cross-charge.
guidance: Revenue Growth: Sustained ~20-22% pace; Margin: Stable EBITDA margins despite expansion; Order Inflow: 10k daily walk-ins (+25% YoY); Capex: INR 380-400cr for 60 new facilities (40 surgical, 20 clinics) in FY27.
order book & pipeline: Pipeline of 30 signed letters of intent for properties; Targeting 7-8 additional Delhi-NCR centers in next 12-18 months.
segment / subsidiary detail: Surgical Services: 67% of revenue, 323k surgeries (+14.5% YoY), Cataract 73% mix (High-end 26.3%, Femto +87%); Refractive 5% mix (SMILE +19%); Non-Surgical (Diagnosis/Consult): 12%; Optical/Pharmacy: 21%. Region: South 61% (+22.6%), West 16% (+19%), North 9% (+20.7%).
growth verticals / optionality: North region doubling facility additions in FY27; Delhi-NCR cluster scaling from 1 to ~8 centers; Mumbai region aggressive push planned; 30% of facilities in Tier-1 vs 63% in other markets offers deep Tier-2/3 penetration runway.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin 30.2% (Q4) despite INR 30cr loss from FY26 vintage centers; Doctor/Employee costs stable at 33% of revenue; Paramedical attrition 21-25% with 9.5-10% wage inflation; New center burn expected to persist at INR 30-40cr level in FY27 due to higher surgical mix additions.
capex / expansion: FY27 Capex guidance INR 380-400cr includes new CMS facility; FY26 acquisition-related payout INR 85cr; FY27 acquisition payout guided at INR 60-65cr; Remaining acquisition liability INR 66cr spread over FY28-FY30.
capital allocation: Debt repayment of INR 195cr completed from IPO proceeds; Focus on organic greenfield growth (60 centers); Merger with subsidiary (AEHL) expected completion by Q3 FY27 (5-6 months post-July EGM).
risks & watch-items: Execution risk in doubling North/West expansion; Regulatory delays in clinical licenses impacting real estate acquisition; Integration risks in pending merger; High paramedical attrition (25%); Concentration risk in South region (61% revenue).
management quality / tone: Confident and execution-focused; Emphasized 'disciplined expansion' and 'operating leverage'; Transparent on new center losses (INR 30cr) as strategic investment; Bullish on premiumization sustainability.
non-obvious takeaways: In-house 'Neo' AI-ready HMS platform managing 20k patients/day built to scale to 5k branches; Own optometry schools mitigate industry-wide talent shortage; Clinical Board ensures standardization across 269 facilities despite rapid geographic dispersion; Femto cataract growth (87%) outpacing overall cataract volume (14%) indicates rapid technology adoption curve.

themes.title: Hospitals, diagnostics & domestic healthcare
themes.need: Under-bedded India plus insurance penetration and preventive-care adoption drive a domestic healthcare capex + volume cycle distinct from export pharma. MAXHEALTH adding ~2,500+ beds (Gurgaon 500-bed by FY27); APOLLOHOSP/MEDANTA/KIMS/NH/ASTERDM/MAXHEALTH on hospitals; LALPATHLAB/METROPOLIS/THYROCARE/VIJAYA on diagnostics (LALPATHLAB guides 13-15% FY27); MEDPLUS/ENTERO on pharmacy/distribution; POLYMED on devices. The same India-only demand engine now also carries India-facing branded pharma, which is driven by domestic volume and price rather than the export book: GLAXO delivered its first INR 1,000cr quarter with 8.1% revenue growth, Shingrix at a ~INR 75cr annual run-rate (CY25, +80% YoY) and Jemperli's first-line approval expanding eligible patients from 800 to 6,000; ERIS (dermatology 15% of revenue after INR 1,265cr of domestic brand acquisitions), SANOFI (India-for-India, NLEM price cuts) and THEMISMED (hospital segment +20% YoY) sit on the same axis.
themes.driver: New-bed commissioning + occupancy ramp; Tier 3/4 diagnostics penetration; CGHS rate revision; preventive-test volumes; domestic branded-formulation volume growth and NLEM/price actions.
